title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: magnetic field, field lines, field due to a current-carrying conductor, field due to a current-carrying coil or solenoid; force on a current-carrying conductor, Fleming's left-hand rule; direct current, alternating current, frequency of AC, advantage of AC over DC; domestic electric circuits.

blocks.title: A compass near a wire
blocks.body:
Put a compass needle under a wire and switch the current on: the needle suddenly turns. Switch it off and the needle swings back. A wire carrying current behaves like a magnet!

This discovery, made by Hans Christian Oersted in 1820, joined electricity and magnetism. In this chapter you will learn about magnetic fields, the fields made by currents, the force on a current in a magnetic field, and how your house is wired safely.

blocks.title: Measuring magnetism in molecules
blocks.body:
Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar, born in Bhera (now in Pakistan), worked on **magnetochemistry**: using magnetic properties to understand how molecules are built. With K. N. Mathur he designed the **Bhatnagar–Mathur magnetic interference balance**.

He was the first Director-General of India's **Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)**, which set up many national laboratories. India's top science award for young scientists, the **Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize**, is named after him.
blocks.future: Electromagnetism leads to careers in electrical engineering, electric vehicles, power distribution, medical imaging (MRI), electronics and the design of motors and speakers.

blocks.question: A compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire turns. What does this tell you?
options: The current produces a magnetic field around the wire
The compass has lost its magnetism
blocks.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet; it turns only in a magnetic field, so the current must be producing one.

blocks.title: The region around a magnet
blocks.body:
A **compass needle** is a small bar magnet; its north-seeking end is the **north pole**. It is deflected near a bar magnet because it experiences a force in the magnet's **magnetic field**, the region around a magnet where its force can be detected. A magnetic field has both **magnitude and direction**.

**Magnetic field lines** (seen with iron filings or traced with a compass):
- Outside the magnet they go from the **north pole to the south pole**; inside, from south to north, so they are **closed curves**.
- The direction of the field at a point is the direction in which a compass north pole would point there.
- Where the lines are **crowded**, the field is **stronger** (near the poles).
- **No two field lines ever cross**: if they did, a compass at that point would have to point in two directions at once.

blocks.question: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect?
options: Field lines exist only inside the magnet
They do cross near the poles
A compass at the crossing would point in two directions at once
blocks.explanation: At any point the field has only one direction, so two lines cannot pass through the same point.

sections.title: Magnetic field due to a current

blocks.title: Wire, loop and solenoid
blocks.body:
**Straight wire:** the field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to it. The field is stronger for a **larger current** and **closer to the wire**. Reversing the current reverses the field. Its direction is given by the **right-hand thumb rule**.

**Circular loop:** each small part of the loop makes circles around itself; near the centre they look like **straight lines**. A coil of n turns gives a field n times as strong as a single turn, because the fields add up.

**Solenoid:** a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder. Its field pattern is like that of a **bar magnet**: one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole. Inside, the field lines are **parallel straight lines**: the field is **uniform**. A soft iron core placed inside makes a strong **electromagnet**, whose magnetism can be switched on and off.

| Rule | Gives | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Right-hand thumb rule | direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire | hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers show the field |
| Fleming's left-hand rule | direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field | stretch thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand at right angles: forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force (motion) |

blocks.question: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is:
blocks.explanation: Inside a solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform.
option_feedback: Inside, it is the same everywhere.
That is around a straight wire.
There is a strong field inside.

blocks.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
blocks.body:
Just as a current exerts a force on a magnet, a magnet exerts an equal and opposite force on a current-carrying conductor (suggested by André-Marie Ampère).

In the activity with an aluminium rod AB hung between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet, the rod is pushed sideways when current flows. Reversing the current, or the field, reverses the push.

- The force is **largest** when the current is **perpendicular** to the magnetic field (and zero when it is parallel).
- The force increases with the **current**, the **strength of the field** and the **length** of the conductor in the field.
- Its direction is given by **Fleming's left-hand rule**: forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current, thumb gives the force.
- A moving charged particle is also a current: a beam of electrons moving one way is a current in the opposite direction.

Devices such as electric motors, loudspeakers and measuring instruments use this force. In medicine, the weak magnetic fields produced inside the body by nerve currents are used for imaging; **MRI** (magnetic resonance imaging) shows the inside of the body.

blocks.question: When is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field the largest?
options: It is the same in all directions
When the current is perpendicular to the field
When the current is parallel to the field
blocks.explanation: The force is maximum when the conductor is at right angles to the field and zero when it is along the field.

blocks.title: How your house is wired
blocks.body:
**AC and DC:** a cell gives **direct current (DC)**, which flows in one direction only. Power stations supply **alternating current (AC)**, which reverses its direction periodically. In India the frequency of AC is **50 Hz**: it changes direction every 1/100 second. The advantage of AC is that it can be transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy.

Electricity reaches the house through the mains at **220 V**, through three wires:

| Wire | Insulation colour | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Live (positive) | red | brings current in at 220 V |
| Neutral (negative) | black | returns the current |
| Earth | green | safety: connects the metal body of an appliance to the ground |

- After the meter and the main **fuse**, there are usually two circuits: a **15 A** circuit for heavy appliances (geyser, air cooler, iron) and a **5 A** circuit for bulbs and fans.
- All appliances are connected in **parallel**, each with its own switch, so each gets the same voltage.
- The **earth wire** connects the metal body of an appliance to a metal plate deep in the ground. If the live wire touches the body, current leaks to the earth, so the user does not get a severe shock.
- A **short circuit** happens when the live wire and the neutral wire come in direct contact (for example through damaged insulation). The resistance falls almost to zero and the current **increases heavily**.
- **Overloading** happens when too many appliances are run from one socket or the supply voltage rises suddenly.
- The **fuse** melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large, preventing damage and fire. Today, **miniature circuit breakers (MCBs)** are also used.

blocks.question: At the time of a short circuit, the current in the circuit:
blocks.explanation: Live and neutral touch directly, the resistance becomes nearly zero, and a very large current flows.
option_feedback: The resistance falls, so the current rises.

sections.title: Rules and safety at a glance

blocks.title: Putting it together
blocks.body:
- **Two ways to produce a magnetic field:** a permanent magnet, and an electric current (a straight wire, a loop, a solenoid or an electromagnet).
- **Two rules, two hands:** the right hand for the field around a current; the left hand for the force on a current.
- **Field strength:** more current, more turns and an iron core give a stronger field.
- **Safety devices:** the fuse (or MCB) and the earth wire.
- **Avoid overloading:** do not connect too many appliances to one socket, and use appliances within the current rating of the circuit.

blocks.question: An electric oven of 2 kW is operated on a 220 V circuit with a current rating of 5 A. What happens?
options: It draws about 9 A, so the fuse blows or the circuit overloads
blocks.explanation: I = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.1 A, more than the 5 A rating.
option_feedback: 9 A is more than the 5 A rating.

blocks.title: Hands and colours
blocks.body:
- **Fleming's left-hand rule, "FBI":** thumb = **F**orce, forefinger = **B** (field), middle finger = **I** (current).
- **Right-hand thumb rule:** thumb = current, curled fingers = field (like gripping a cricket bat).
- **Wire colours:** **R**ed = **R**isky live; **B**lack = **B**ack (neutral); **G**reen = **G**round (earth).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Using the right hand for the force on a conductor: the force needs the **left** hand.
- Forgetting that a beam of electrons is a current in the **opposite** direction.
- Saying field lines go from south to north outside a magnet: outside, they go from **north to south**.
- Writing that the earth wire carries current all the time: it carries current only when there is a leakage.
- Saying that a fuse is connected in parallel: it is in series with the live wire.

blocks.title: Try it in class
blocks.body: Sprinkle iron filings on a card over a bar magnet and tap it to show field lines; repeat with a thick wire passing through the card connected to a battery for a moment to show circles. Wind insulated wire round an iron nail, connect a cell, and pick up pins: a simple electromagnet. Show students the three coloured wires in a plug top, with the supply switched off.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend how the earth wire protects us from a shock, and how a fuse protects the house from a fire.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 11:** current, resistance and power; the fuse uses the heating effect.
- **Class 12 Physics:** moving charges and magnetism, electromagnetic induction, alternating current and motors.
- **Everyday life:** electric fans, mixers, loudspeakers, MRI machines and the wiring of every house.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
A positively charged particle (alpha particle) is projected towards the west and is deflected towards the north by a magnetic field.

(a) What is the direction of the field? (b) Which rule did you use? (c) What would happen to an electron moving the same way in the same field?

**Answer:** (a) Upward (vertically up). (b) Fleming's left-hand rule: middle finger (current) towards the west, thumb (force) towards the north, so the forefinger (field) points upward. (c) An electron moving west is a current towards the east, so it is pushed the opposite way: towards the south.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- A magnetic field has magnitude and direction; field lines go from north to south outside a magnet, are closed curves, are crowded where the field is strong, and never cross.
- A current produces a magnetic field: concentric circles around a straight wire (right-hand thumb rule), straight lines at the centre of a loop, and a uniform field inside a solenoid.
- A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force, largest when perpendicular to the field; direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
- India's mains supply is AC at 220 V and 50 Hz; houses use live, neutral and earth wires, parallel connections, fuses and MCBs.
- Short circuits and overloading cause very large currents; fuses and earthing protect us.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Practise diagrams: field lines of a bar magnet, a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid, and a domestic circuit with fuse and earth wire.
- Learn to state both rules with the finger meanings.
- For direction questions, convert electron motion into current direction first.
- Know the colours of the three wires and the ratings 5 A and 15 A.

blocks.front: Shape of the field lines around a straight current-carrying wire
blocks.back: Concentric circles centred on the wire.
Green (live is red, neutral is black).
